slides.title: Where the parameters live
slides.body:
If you sum up the parameters in a transformer layer, the **FFN (feed-forward network)** is bigger than attention. For a typical configuration with hidden size `d_model = 4096` and FFN expansion factor 4, the FFN has:

- `W_1`: [4096, 16384] = 67M parameters
- `W_2`: [16384, 4096] = 67M parameters

...vs attention's three projections + output, each [4096, 4096] = 16M each, totaling 67M.

In the standard architecture, FFN takes ~2/3 of the parameter budget per layer. It's also where most of the FLOPs go. Attention gets the headlines because it does the cross-token mixing; FFN is where the model actually stores and applies its learned knowledge.

slides.title: What FFN actually computes
slides.body:
The FFN is a 2-layer MLP applied **independently to each token position**:

$$\text{FFN}(x) = W_2 \cdot \text{activation}(W_1 \cdot x + b_1) + b_2$$

For each token vector `x` (shape `[d_model]`):
1. **Up-project** to a wider hidden dim (typically 4× `d_model`).
2. Apply a **non-linear activation** (originally ReLU; modern models use GELU or SwiGLU).
3. **Down-project** back to `d_model`.

The critical detail: **there is no cross-token interaction inside FFN.** Token at position 5 is processed without ever seeing token at position 4 or 6. All cross-token mixing happens in attention; FFN is the per-token nonlinearity.

This is sometimes summarized as: *attention mixes tokens; FFN mixes features.*

question.question: Inside the FFN block, can token i's output depend on token j's input?
options: Yes — that's the whole point of the transformer
Yes, but only within an attention window
No — the FFN is applied independently to each token; cross-token mixing happens only in attention
Only when the FFN uses GELU activation
question.explanation: FFN is per-token. The same MLP weights are applied to each position, but each position's computation is independent. If you removed all attention layers and kept only FFNs, the model would lose all ability to use context — the FFN would map each input embedding to an output without ever seeing any other token.

slides.title: Why 4× expansion
slides.body:
The expansion factor (`d_ff / d_model`) is a design choice. The original transformer used 4. Most modern models still use 4 (or close — LLaMA uses ~2.7 with SwiGLU because the gating costs an extra projection).

Why 4? Empirically, 4 hits a sweet spot: smaller and the FFN can't represent rich enough nonlinearities; larger and you're spending parameters that didn't help.

Intuition for why **larger** FFN matters: the up-projection moves each token into a higher-dimensional space where features can be linearly separable. The activation function picks out the right features. The down-projection collapses back. The 4× ratio gives the model enough room to do this for the kinds of features it needs to learn.

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) breaks this rule: each MoE FFN is much larger than 4×, but only one (or a few) experts is active per token, so the per-token compute stays similar.

slides.title: GELU and SwiGLU
slides.body:
Activation functions have evolved:

**ReLU** (original transformer): `max(0, x)`. Simple, fast, but has dead neurons (always-zero gradient when negative).

**GELU** (BERT, GPT-2): `x * Φ(x)` where Φ is the standard normal CDF. Smooth, slightly negative for slightly-negative `x`, mostly positive for positive `x`. Helps gradient flow; consistently outperformed ReLU in language modeling.

**SwiGLU** (LLaMA, modern Mistral, etc.): a *gated* variant. Splits the up-projection into two halves, applies a sigmoid-like gating function (Swish) to one half, multiplies by the other:

$$\text{SwiGLU}(x) = (\text{Swish}(xW) \odot xV) W_2$$

The gating means the FFN can selectively activate features based on the input. SwiGLU consistently beats GELU at the same compute budget, which is why it's the default in 2024+ models.

question.question: If you ablated all FFN layers and kept only attention, what would happen?
options: The model would still work, just be slightly less accurate
The model could still mix tokens (via attention) but couldn't transform per-token features beyond linear combinations of values; capacity would drop dramatically
Attention would automatically take over the FFN's role
The model would refuse to train
question.explanation: Attention is largely linear (with the softmax doing weighted averaging). Without the FFN's nonlinearity, the per-token transformation is mostly a linear combination of input values. The model loses most of its ability to compute non-trivial per-token functions; quality drops sharply even though token mixing still works.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
FFN is the parameter sink and the per-token nonlinearity. With attention + FFN, you have the two building blocks of every transformer layer. The next pieces are the glue: [[residual-connections]] (so deep stacks remain trainable) and [[layer-normalization]] (so activations stay well-scaled).

Key takeaways:
- FFN holds ~2/3 of a transformer layer's parameters
- It's per-token; all cross-token mixing happens in attention
- 4× expansion is the empirical sweet spot
- SwiGLU has become the default activation; GELU is the previous-generation choice
